title: MAO Inhibitors: Hypertensive Crisis and Serotonin Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors have extensive food and drug interactions. Tyramine exposure can precipitate severe hypertension, while serotonergic or sympathomimetic combinations can cause serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis; required washout intervals must be respected when switching therapies.
recognize: Severe occipital headache, palpitations, marked hypertension, chest pain, neck stiffness, nausea, or diaphoresis can signal hypertensive crisis.
Clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, fever, and diarrhea suggest serotonin syndrome.
priorities: Review all prescriptions, OTC decongestants/stimulants, supplements, and planned antidepressant changes.
Teach the prescribed tyramine-restricted diet and medication-interaction list.
Escalate hypertensive-crisis or serotonin-syndrome symptoms immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, headache, autonomic/neuromuscular symptoms, adherence, and medication/food exposures.
interventions: During suspected severe interaction, stop the precipitating agents under emergency direction and provide monitored supportive care.
medicationSafety: SSRIs, SNRIs, many TCAs, meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, stimulants, and sympathomimetics can be dangerous with MAOIs.
Switching antidepressants requires drug-specific washout intervals; fluoxetine requires particular caution because of its long half-life.
redFlags: Severe headache with marked BP elevation
teaching: Carry an interaction list, avoid prohibited high-tyramine foods, and check before taking OTC cold/cough products.
delegationScope: Suspected hypertensive or serotonergic toxicity requires immediate licensed-nurse/emergency escalation.
examTrap: Recommending an OTC decongestant to a patient taking an MAOI without checking interactions.
oneLinePearl: MAOI safety lives in the interaction list—food, OTC drugs, and antidepressant washouts.

title: Bupropion: Seizure Risk and Smoking-Cessation Safety
bottomLine: Bupropion is used for depression and smoking cessation and has little sexual dysfunction compared with many serotonergic antidepressants, but it lowers seizure threshold. It is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in current/prior bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of seizure risk.
recognize: Insomnia, dry mouth, agitation, tremor, and increased BP can occur.
Risk rises with high doses, abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, eating disorders, head injury, and other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs.
priorities: Screen for seizure/eating-disorder history and abrupt sedative/alcohol withdrawal risk.
Monitor mood/suicidality and BP in susceptible patients.
Give doses early enough to reduce insomnia according to the prescribed formulation schedule.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, suicidal thinking, sleep, BP, tobacco use, neurologic symptoms, and adherence.
interventions: For smoking cessation, combine medication with behavioral support and a quit plan.
medicationSafety: Do not crush sustained/extended-release formulations.
Avoid duplicating bupropion-containing products prescribed under different brand names/indications.
teaching: Do not double missed doses, avoid abrupt alcohol/sedative withdrawal, and report seizures or severe mood changes.
delegationScope: New seizure or major mood deterioration requires licensed-nurse/provider escalation.
examTrap: Choosing bupropion for a patient with bulimia because weight gain and sexual side effects are lower.
oneLinePearl: Bupropion avoids many serotonin effects but lowers the seizure threshold.

title: Buspirone: Delayed Anxiolysis, Not PRN Rescue
bottomLine: Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic used for generalized anxiety. It does not provide immediate PRN relief; benefit develops over days to weeks, so regular scheduled adherence matters.
recognize: Dizziness, headache, nausea, and nervousness can occur early.
Unlike benzodiazepines, buspirone has much less sedative and dependence potential but does not treat benzodiazepine withdrawal.
priorities: Teach scheduled use and realistic onset expectations.
Review MAOI and serotonergic medications and grapefruit/product interaction instructions.
Assess dizziness/fall risk during initiation.
assessMonitor: Trend anxiety symptoms over weeks, dizziness, adherence, BP when interacting drugs are present, and serotonin-toxicity symptoms.
interventions: Combine with psychotherapy, sleep, and behavioral anxiety-management strategies when appropriate.
medicationSafety: MAOI combinations can cause dangerous BP reactions and require separation according to labeling.
Use consistently with or without food because food changes absorption.
teaching: Take it every day as prescribed; do not expect a dose taken during a panic episode to work like a benzodiazepine.
delegationScope: Severe interaction symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Offering buspirone as a rapid PRN medication for an acute panic attack.
oneLinePearl: Buspirone is scheduled anxiety control, not instant rescue.

title: Donepezil: Cognition Support With Bradycardia and GI Risk
bottomLine: Donepezil is a cholinesterase inhibitor that may modestly support cognition/function in Alzheimer disease but does not reverse the disease. Monitor for nausea/diarrhea, weight loss, bradycardia/syncope, sleep disturbance, and GI bleeding risk in susceptible patients.
recognize: Cholinergic effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, sweating, bradycardia, and vivid dreams.
Falls or unexplained syncope may reflect bradyarrhythmia rather than only dementia progression.
priorities: Assess pulse, syncope/falls, weight/nutrition, GI symptoms, and interacting bradycardic drugs.
Reinforce realistic expectations and caregiver support.
Escalate symptomatic bradycardia, GI bleeding, or severe weight loss.
assessMonitor: Trend cognition/function, pulse, falls, weight, appetite, stool/GI symptoms, sleep, and caregiver observations.
interventions: Use fall precautions and nutrition support when adverse effects threaten safety.
medicationSafety: Beta blockers and other heart-rate-lowering drugs may compound bradycardia.
NSAIDs can add GI bleeding risk in susceptible patients.
teaching: The goal is maintaining function, not curing dementia; report fainting, black stools, or substantial weight loss.
delegationScope: Routine functional observations may be delegated, but syncope/bradycardia/GI bleeding require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Interpreting new syncope as dementia behavior without checking the pulse and medication effects.
oneLinePearl: Donepezil can help cognition modestly but can slow the heart noticeably.

title: Memantine: Moderate-Severe Alzheimer Symptom Management
bottomLine: Memantine is an NMDA-receptor antagonist used for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. It may support cognition/function but does not stop neurodegeneration; dizziness, confusion, constipation, BP effects, and renal-dose considerations are practical nursing concerns.
recognize: Dizziness and confusion can increase fall risk.
Renal impairment can require dose adjustment because elimination is substantially renal.
priorities: Assess renal function, falls/dizziness, cognition/function, bowel pattern, and adherence.
Differentiate medication adverse effects from acute delirium or progression.
Escalate abrupt mental-status change rather than attributing it automatically to dementia.
assessMonitor: Trend cognition/function, dizziness, falls, BP, constipation, renal function, and caregiver observations.
interventions: Use fall prevention and bowel support as appropriate and maintain structured routines.
medicationSafety: Urine alkalinization can reduce memantine clearance and increase concentrations.
Dose adjustment may be required in severe renal impairment.
teaching: Expect symptom support rather than cure and report sudden changes from baseline.
delegationScope: Acute cognition changes require licensed-nurse assessment; routine function observations can support trend monitoring.
examTrap: Assuming sudden confusion after a dose change is inevitable Alzheimer progression.
oneLinePearl: Memantine supports function; sudden decline still demands an acute-cause search.

title: Levetiracetam: Seizure Control and Behavioral Changes
bottomLine: Levetiracetam is a common antiseizure medication with relatively few pharmacokinetic interactions, but sedation, dizziness, and significant behavioral or mood changes can occur. Renal impairment requires dose consideration.
recognize: Irritability, aggression, depression, anxiety, psychotic symptoms, or suicidal thinking can emerge or worsen.
Somnolence and dizziness increase fall risk.
priorities: Assess seizure frequency, renal function, sedation, mood, aggression, and suicidal thinking.
Do not abruptly discontinue chronic therapy because seizures can worsen.
Escalate dangerous behavioral changes or suicidal intent promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend seizures, adherence, mood/behavior, falls, renal function, and sedation.
interventions: Use fall precautions during initiation/dose changes and coordinate behavioral safety support if symptoms emerge.
medicationSafety: Renal clearance requires dose adjustment in impairment.
Other CNS depressants can increase sedation even though metabolic interactions are limited.
teaching: Report major mood or behavior changes and do not stop suddenly even if seizure-free.
delegationScope: Behavioral deterioration or seizure escalation requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Ignoring new aggression or suicidal thoughts because levetiracetam has fewer drug interactions than older antiseizure medications.
oneLinePearl: Levetiracetam is interaction-light but behavior-heavy for some patients.

title: Oral Bisphosphonates: Empty Stomach and Upright Safety
bottomLine: Oral bisphosphonates reduce fracture risk in selected osteoporosis patients but have strict administration requirements to improve absorption and reduce esophageal injury: take with plain water on an empty stomach and remain upright for the product-specified interval before food, beverages, or other medications.
recognize: New severe heartburn, odynophagia, or chest pain can signal esophageal injury.
Jaw problems and persistent thigh/groin pain can signal rare osteonecrosis or atypical femur fracture.
priorities: Confirm the patient can remain upright and follow administration instructions.
Assess renal function, calcium/vitamin D plan, dental problems, swallowing/esophageal disorders, and adherence.
Escalate severe esophageal symptoms, jaw necrosis concern, or new thigh/groin pain.
assessMonitor: Trend fractures, bone-density follow-up, calcium/vitamin D status when ordered, renal function, GI tolerance, dental health, and musculoskeletal pain.
interventions: Pair pharmacotherapy with fall prevention, weight-bearing/resistance activity, smoking cessation, and adequate nutrition.
medicationSafety: Calcium, antacids, food, and many beverages greatly reduce oral absorption when taken too close to the dose.
Hypocalcemia should be corrected before therapy according to the treatment plan.
teaching: Follow product-specific empty-stomach/upright instructions exactly and report new jaw or thigh pain.
delegationScope: Administration teaching may be reinforced by the care team; severe adverse-effect symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving alendronate with breakfast, coffee, and calcium supplements to improve tolerance.
oneLinePearl: Bisphosphonate morning rule: plain water, empty stomach, stay upright.
sourceBasis: Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation guidance

title: Naloxone: Reverse Opioid Respiratory Depression, Then Reassess
bottomLine: Naloxone reverses opioid effects, especially respiratory depression, but its duration can be shorter than the opioid's. Airway/ventilation support and repeated reassessment are mandatory because respiratory depression can recur after initial awakening.
recognize: Opioid toxicity often presents with slow/shallow breathing, decreased consciousness, and miosis, though pupils are not reliable enough to delay treatment.
Withdrawal after naloxone can cause agitation, vomiting, tachycardia, pain, and sympathetic stress.
priorities: Call for emergency help and support ventilation/oxygenation first.
Administer naloxone by the available approved route according to protocol.
Reassess respiratory rate/effort and consciousness continuously and repeat treatment when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend breathing, oxygenation, consciousness, recurrence, aspiration/vomiting, withdrawal, and suspected opioid type/route.
interventions: Use rescue breathing/BVM ventilation when needed rather than waiting for naloxone to work.
medicationSafety: Long-acting opioids and potent synthetic opioids may require repeated naloxone dosing or infusion under advanced care.
The treatment goal is adequate ventilation, not necessarily complete reversal of all analgesia or sedation.
teaching: After community naloxone use, call emergency services and stay with the person because the opioid can outlast naloxone.
delegationScope: Community/protocol naloxone use may be broadly authorized, but severe opioid toxicity requires immediate licensed/emergency assessment.
examTrap: Leaving the patient alone once they wake up after naloxone.
oneLinePearl: Naloxone may wear off first—ventilate, reverse, reassess, repeat.

title: Epinephrine for Anaphylaxis: IM First-Line Treatment
bottomLine: Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Airway swelling, wheeze, hypotension, or rapidly progressive multisystem allergic symptoms should trigger immediate IM epinephrine and emergency response; antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and must not delay it.
recognize: Anaphylaxis can occur without hives.
Respiratory compromise, hypotension, or involvement of multiple organ systems after a likely allergen are key clues.
priorities: Give IM epinephrine promptly in the anterolateral thigh according to emergency protocol.
Call for emergency help, support airway/oxygenation/ventilation, and give IV fluids for shock as indicated.
Repeat epinephrine according to response/protocol when symptoms persist.
assessMonitor: Trend airway swelling, wheeze, oxygenation, BP, pulse, skin/GI symptoms, and recurrence after initial improvement.
interventions: Position supine with legs elevated when tolerated in hypotension; modify for respiratory distress, vomiting, pregnancy, or other clinical needs.
medicationSafety: There is no absolute contraindication to IM epinephrine in life-threatening anaphylaxis.
IV epinephrine bolus dosing carries substantial arrhythmia/hypertension risk and belongs to advanced monitored protocols.
teaching: Patients prescribed autoinjectors should carry them, know the technique, use epinephrine promptly for anaphylaxis, and seek emergency care afterward.
delegationScope: Emergency epinephrine authority varies by protocol/setting but treatment should not be delayed by waiting for antihistamines or nonessential steps.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first while a hypotensive wheezing patient with tongue swelling deteriorates.

title: Oxytocin: Uterine Tachysystole and Fetal Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions and is used for induction/augmentation and postpartum hemorrhage management. During labor, excessive uterine activity can reduce uteroplacental perfusion and cause fetal compromise; infusion management requires continuous maternal-fetal assessment and facility-defined competency.
recognize: Tachysystole or prolonged/tetanic contractions with recurrent fetal decelerations suggest excessive uterine stimulation.
Prolonged high-dose infusion can rarely contribute to water intoxication because oxytocin has antidiuretic effects.
priorities: Monitor contraction frequency/duration, resting tone when available, fetal heart pattern, maternal BP/pulse, and fluid balance.
Reduce/stop oxytocin and initiate intrauterine resuscitative measures according to protocol when tachysystole or fetal compromise develops.
Escalate persistent abnormal fetal status or suspected uterine rupture immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend fetal heart baseline/variability/decelerations, contraction pattern, maternal vital signs, intake/output, sodium when prolonged/high exposure is clinically concerning, and postpartum uterine response.
interventions: Use a controlled infusion pump and dedicated line setup per facility protocol.
Position to optimize uteroplacental perfusion and correct maternal hypotension/excessive uterine activity according to orders.
medicationSafety: Excess oxytocin can cause uterine tachysystole, fetal hypoxia, uterine rupture, and postpartum hemorrhage from uterine fatigue.
Water intoxication with seizure/coma is a rare but serious complication of prolonged high exposure.
redFlags: Recurrent late decelerations with loss of variability
Sudden severe abdominal pain with loss of station
teaching: Explain that contraction and fetal monitoring are required because the dose is adjusted to both uterine response and fetal tolerance.
delegationScope: Oxytocin initiation/titration authority varies by state/facility and generally requires obstetric competency; PN/LVN roles may center on monitoring, recognition, and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Continuing to increase oxytocin because labor is slow despite uterine tachysystole and recurrent late decelerations.
oneLinePearl: Oxytocin works only when contractions improve labor without sacrificing fetal perfusion.
sourceBasis: ACOG 2025 intrapartum fetal heart rate guidance
